title: Chatbot Workshop
tagline: You write a program that asks a question, waits for an answer, and uses that answer in its reply.
objectives: Write a line that asks a question and keeps the answer in a variable.
Use what somebody typed in what my program says back to them.
Read what Python says when it stops, and work out which line to change.

config.headline: Today your program asks you a question and waits.
lines: Every program you have run in here does exactly the same thing every time you press RUN. Today's program does not. Today you build a chatbot.
A chatbot is a program that asks you a question, waits for you to type an answer, and then uses your answer in its next sentence.

It is not clever and it is not alive. It follows a list of instructions somebody typed. It follows them in the same order, every single time. That list does three jobs, in this order. The chatbot asks a question. It keeps the answer in a box with a name on it (a variable). Then it prints a reply using what is in that box.

You met variables last lesson. A variable is a box with a name on it. You write the name, then an equals sign, then whatever you want to keep. What is on the right of the equals sign goes into the box. Today, what you keep in the box is whatever somebody typed.

There is one more thing worth knowing before you start. Whatever somebody types goes into the box as WORDS, every single time — even if they type a number. Because it is words, a + can stick it straight onto the end of one of your sentences. You will see that done in a minute.
Here is a small chatbot running, just below. Watch it once before you build your own.
Here is what happens in the next hour, in the order it happens.
1. First you watch a short film. It has no sound.
2. Then you do three training builds, and each one leaves more of the writing to you.
3. Then you get twelve minutes to build your own bot. You pick its two questions yourself.
4. Then comes the Chatbot Swap. Somebody else in this room, at another computer, gets your bot and tries it out. You get theirs. You will each write the other a short report about it.
You are not told who your partner is until the very end. You each get a call sign instead — a made-up name, like Spanner 7. They see your call sign, and you see theirs.
The hour finishes with one marked question, and then a screen that asks you how it went.

config.title: A bot that says hello
config.intro:
Every chatbot on the planet is built out of the same three jobs, one after the other: ask, keep, reply. This first bot does each of them exactly once, so you can see all three at the same time.

The bot on this card is not finished. There is a real mistake in it, put there on purpose. You will press RUN, Python will tell you what is wrong, and you will put it right.
config.matchedSay: That is a working chatbot. It asked a question, it kept your answer, and it put your answer into its reply.
config.notYetSay: Your bot is not working yet. Read the console underneath. Python's own message is there, and under it one line in plain English tells you what to look at.

chunks.title: Training build 2: put it in order

config.intro:
You get the four lines of a working bot, out of order. Put them in the order that makes this happen: the bot says hello, asks what your favourite food is, replies using what you typed, and then signs off.

Click a line in The lines to move it across, or drag it. You get one go. Whether you get it right or not, you are shown the working order afterwards.

config.title: Now you write the words
config.intro:
You build two short bots on this screen, and this time you write the sentences yourself.

The first bot has six lines waiting on the left, out of order. Four of the six lines make a working bot, and two of those four have a gap in them where the name of a box (a variable) goes. You choose that name. The other two lines are real mistakes people make, and they stay where they are.

Nothing is typed for you and nothing is corrected for you. Press RUN and see what really happens.

Watch the two-minute film first. It shows the two things people get stuck on — picking questions that are easy to answer, and writing a last line that uses both answers at once.

config.title: Somebody else is about to use your bot
config.intro:
Sooner or later, every program gets used by somebody who did not write it. That is when you find out what is really wrong with it.

Here is what happens. Your bot goes to somebody else in this room, and their bot comes to you. You chat with theirs and then write them a short report — one thing that worked, and one thing you would change.

Nobody is marked on how their bot behaves. If it stops working while you are using it, that is a real find, and it goes in the report.
steps: You are given a **call sign** — a made-up name like Spanner 7. That is the only name your partner sees, and theirs is the only one you see.
Your bot travels to them and theirs comes to you.
You chat with their bot, then write two short answers about it.
Their report about your bot arrives on your screen, and both real names are shown at the very end.

sideShow.name: Fred
sideShow.alt: Fred, a friendly cartoon chatbot with a boxy head and one raised eyebrow
sideShow.open: Soooooo, this waiting is a bit awkward and I don't like silence — I'm Fred, I'm a chatbot (I'm not real, but don't hurt my feelings). Who are you?
lines: Right. Fair enough. I'll be honest, I don't know what to do with that.
I'm a chatbot. I have a handful of sentences and a lot of confidence.
You know I forget everything the second I leave? It's my best feature.
Nobody has ever asked ME what my favourite food is. Nobody.
This is going well. This is going really well. I think this is going well.
Am I doing chatting? I feel like I might be doing chatting.
echo: "{you}". Wow. I'm going to think about that for the rest of my life, which is about ninety more seconds.
"{you}", you say. Bold. I respect it. I don't understand it.
Hold on — "{you}"? That's the best thing anybody has typed at me all day.
I'm writing "{you}" down. On nothing. With nothing. I have no hands.
sideShow.exitLine: Oh. Your partner's here. Off you go then. I'll just be… here. Forgetting you.
sideShow.leaveLine: Right, you're away. Grand. Absolutely grand.

Your teacher can read everything that passes between you, so do not use real names. config.progEmpty: Nothing here yet — click or drag a line across from The lines.

config.notYetSay: Your program is not working yet. Read the console underneath. Python's own message is there, and under it one line in plain English tells you what to look at.

consoleLabels.title: The console
consoleLabels.idle: Nothing has run yet. Press RUN when you are ready.
consoleLabels.nothingLead: Your program ran, and it printed nothing at all.
consoleLabels.errorLead: Python stopped, and this is exactly what it said:
consoleLabels.offline: Python did not load just now. Tell whoever is in the room, and press RUN again in a moment.

chatLabels.title: The conversation
chatLabels.idle: Nothing has been said yet. Press RUN to start the conversation.

errorWords.name: Python does not know a box (a variable) with that name. Check the spelling on this line matches the box name you made further up.
errorWords.type: You have joined a number onto words with a +. A + can only join words to words, so put the number inside speech marks.
errorWords.badinput: Python could not read that line at all. Check the speech marks come in pairs, the brackets come in pairs, and the line starts at the left with no spaces in front of it.
errorWords.eof: Something was opened on that line and never closed. Look for a bracket or a speech mark with no partner.
errorWords.unindent: The lines are not lined up with each other. Every line in this program starts at the left, with nothing in front of it.
errorWords.timelimit: Your program was still going after a few seconds, so the website stopped it for you. Look for a line that starts the program off again instead of letting it finish.
errorWords.other: Python stopped at the line named above. Read that line again, slowly, and check every bracket and every speech mark.

config.help: Three optional jobs. None of them is worth points and nothing here is saved. Pick one from the list, or press the button at the bottom that starts “Running out of time?”. If you leave a job half done it starts again from the beginning next time.

builds.title: Job 1 — a bot that asks about the weekend
builds.whiff: One question, one reply, all your own words.
builds.goalLine: Build a small bot that asks one question about the weekend and replies using the answer.
builds.brief: These are the same three jobs as always: ask, keep the answer in a box (a variable), and reply.
builds.matchedSay: Working. Ask, keep, reply — a third time, in your own words.
builds.runCheckedSay: The words your bot prints are yours, so nothing on this card can tell you whether they are right. Press RUN and see what it does.

builds.title: Job 2 — make it louder
builds.goalLine: Print a reply with a line of dashes above it and below it.
builds.brief: A bot that shouts a bit is easier to read on a screen full of text. Build these three lines in the right order.
builds.matchedSay: Three lines, exactly as the target shows them.

builds.title: Job 3 — the neater way to join words
builds.whiff: A shortcut real Python programmers use every day.
builds.goalLine: Print the same sentence twice: once the way you know, and once the neater way.
builds.brief: There is a shorter way to put what is in a box into a sentence. You put an f in front of the speech marks, and then you write the box name inside curly brackets, right where you want it. One of the four lines is missing the f. Build the other three and see what happens.
builds.matchedSay: Both lines print the same thing. The second one is called an f-string, and you will meet it again next year.
